title: Adverse Drug Reactions, Allergies, Interactions & Medication Reconciliation
html:
Medication safety does not end after the correct dose reaches the correct client. The RN must recognize harm early, distinguish allergy from predictable effects and disease change, identify interacting exposures, and keep one accurate medication story across every transition. The safest response is client-centered: stabilize urgent threats, stop or hold suspected exposure when clinically appropriate, notify the right team, document facts, and create a follow-up plan that prevents re-exposure without denying useful treatment.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate adverse drug events, adverse drug reactions, side effects, intolerance, allergy, toxicity, and medication errors.
  • Recognize anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous adverse reactions, organ injury, and dangerous withdrawal.
  • Analyze drug–drug, drug–food, drug–condition, and duplicate-ingredient interactions.
  • Build and reconcile a best possible medication history at admission, transfer, and discharge.
  • Respond to suspected medication harm and report it through appropriate clinical and safety channels.
  • Teach a clear, usable medication plan with urgent warning signs and follow-up.

Name the event accurately

An adverse drug event (ADE) is harm involving medication use; it may result from a reaction, an error, an overdose, an interaction, or failure to monitor. An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful or unintended response reasonably associated with a medicine at normally used doses. A side effect is a known secondary effect that may be expected and may or may not require a change. Intolerance describes an unpleasant, often predictable effect that limits use but is not necessarily immune mediated.

A drug allergy implies an immune-mediated reaction. Toxicity reflects excessive exposure or vulnerability, such as renal accumulation. A medication error is a preventable failure in prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparation, administration, monitoring, or communication; it may reach the client with or without causing harm. A near miss is still valuable safety information.

A symptom label is not enough
Record the exact drug, dose and route, timing, signs and symptoms, severity, treatment, and outcome. “Allergy: unknown” can cause both dangerous re-exposure and unnecessary avoidance.

First decide whether the client is unstable

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, vital signs, oxygenation, skin and mucosa, and the timing of symptoms relative to medication exposure. Stop an active infusion or withhold the next dose when a severe reaction is suspected and doing so is within the emergency protocol; maintain appropriate access and call for help. Do not delay emergency treatment while proving causality.

Escalate immediately for airway swelling, stridor, wheeze, hypoxemia, hypotension, shock, severe blistering or mucosal lesions, rapidly spreading rash with systemic illness, seizure, severe dysrhythmia, major bleeding, profound hypoglycemia, hyperthermia with rigidity or clonus, acute liver failure, anuria, or rapidly worsening neurologic status. Supportive actions and antidotes follow current orders and protocols.

Anaphylaxis is a clinical emergency

Anaphylaxis may involve hives or flushing, but skin findings can be absent. Suspect it after a likely exposure when airway compromise, bronchospasm, hypotension, collapse, or a rapid combination of skin, respiratory, circulatory, and gastrointestinal findings appears. Stop the suspected exposure, activate emergency response, and support airway, breathing, and circulation.

Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line treatment under the emergency protocol; antihistamines and corticosteroids do not replace it for airway or circulatory compromise. Positioning, oxygen, IV fluids, repeat epinephrine, bronchodilation, and advanced support depend on the clinical response and protocol. Observe for recurrence and update the reaction record before transition.

Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

Fever, facial edema, painful skin, blistering, skin detachment, target-like lesions, oral or eye erosions, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, or liver and kidney injury after a medicine may signal Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, or another severe cutaneous adverse reaction. Stop further exposure to the suspected drug under urgent clinical direction, protect the airway and mucosa, assess fluids and organs, and obtain specialist or emergency care. Do not reassure a client with mucosal lesions that the eruption is a simple rash.

Organ toxicity can look like disease progression

Trend symptoms with medication starts, stops, and dose changes. Acute kidney injury may follow nephrotoxins, dehydration, or interactions; hepatotoxicity may present with fatigue, nausea, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, or rising enzymes; marrow suppression can cause infection, bleeding, or anemia; QT prolongation can lead to syncope and torsades; CNS depression can impair ventilation; and anticoagulant effects can cause occult or visible bleeding.

Risk is shaped by dose, duration, age, pregnancy, genetics, allergies, kidney and liver function, volume status, nutrition, alcohol, comorbidities, and other products. A previously tolerated dose can become unsafe during acute illness or after an interacting medicine is added.

Interactions are more than two prescriptions

A drug–drug interaction may raise exposure and toxicity, reduce exposure and effectiveness, or produce additive effects such as sedation, bleeding, hypotension, QT prolongation, serotonin excess, or potassium disturbance. A drug–food or beverage interaction can involve alcohol, grapefruit, vitamin K intake, tyramine, minerals, or tube feeding, depending on the exact medicine. A drug–condition interaction occurs when a disease or physiologic state changes safety, such as an NSAID in active GI bleeding or renal injury.

Include OTC medicines, supplements, herbals, cannabis, alcohol, nicotine, energy products, topical products, drops, inhalers, injections, and medicines obtained outside the usual health system. Look for duplicate ingredients across combination cold, pain, and sleep products. Interaction databases support—not replace—assessment of the actual client, dose, route, timing, and clinical consequence.

Enzyme inhibition, induction, and pharmacodynamic stacking

Metabolic or transporter inhibition can raise the substrate concentration and toxicity, sometimes quickly. Induction can lower exposure and efficacy and may take time to develop or fade. The clinical effect varies with the exact pathway, therapeutic window, and client factors. Never memorize one interaction without verifying current labeling for the precise products.

Pharmacodynamic stacking occurs when different drugs produce the same harmful effect without changing each other’s concentrations. Examples include opioids plus benzodiazepines or alcohol suppressing ventilation; anticoagulants plus antiplatelets or NSAIDs increasing bleeding; several QT-prolonging medicines plus low potassium increasing dysrhythmia risk; and multiple anticholinergic medicines worsening retention or delirium.

Build the best possible medication history

Ask open-endedly what the client actually takes, then use multiple sources when available: client and caregiver interview with permission, medication bottles or photographs, pharmacy fill history, outpatient records, previous discharge lists, administration records, and prescriber information. No single source proves current use.

For every prescription and nonprescription product, record name, formulation, strength, dose, route, schedule, indication, actual pattern, last dose, recent changes, prescriber, benefit, problems, and access. Ask directly about insulin, inhalers, patches, eye drops, creams, injections, contraceptives, anticoagulants, steroids, PRN drugs, supplements, and medicines taken weekly or monthly. Clarify allergies and reactions separately.

Reconciliation means compare, decide, and communicate

Medication reconciliation compares the complete pretransition regimen with new admission, transfer, procedure, or discharge orders. Identify omissions, duplications, dose or route changes, wrong frequencies, stopped drugs that were unintentionally resumed, continued drugs that should be held, interactions, contraindications, therapeutic substitutions, and incomplete monitoring. Every discrepancy is classified as intentional and documented or unintentional and resolved with an authorized prescriber.

A medication list copied forward without comparison is not reconciliation. High-risk transitions deserve extra attention: emergency admission, surgery, intensive care transfer, discharge, dialysis, pregnancy, pediatrics, older age, polypharmacy, cognitive or language barriers, and care split across multiple systems.

One accurate medication story must survive every handoff
The receiving team and the client need to know exactly what was started, changed, held, continued, or stopped—and why.

Admission, transfer, and discharge have different risks

At admission, distinguish the home regimen from inpatient orders and identify the last dose. A medicine may be intentionally held because of illness or procedure; document the reason and review plan. At internal transfer, protect time-critical medicines, tapers, infusions, anticoagulation, insulin, antimicrobials, seizure therapy, and monitoring requirements from accidental interruption.

At discharge, create one final list that clearly marks starts, stops, changes, and continuations. Resolve duplicate prescriptions and conflicting instructions before the client leaves. Send the list to the next clinician or facility through the approved process and reconcile it with the pharmacy plan, access, equipment, laboratory follow-up, and scheduled appointments.

Withdrawal and rebound are medication harms too

Stopping exposure may be lifesaving during anaphylaxis or toxicity, but abrupt discontinuation of some medicines can cause harm. Benzodiazepines and antiseizure medicines may precipitate seizures; corticosteroids may cause adrenal crisis; beta blockers or clonidine may cause cardiovascular rebound; opioids may cause withdrawal; and antidepressants may cause discontinuation symptoms. The urgent threat determines the immediate response, followed by a drug-specific taper, substitution, or monitoring plan.

Respond to a suspected adverse drug event

  1. Stabilize the client and stop or hold the suspected exposure when indicated.
  2. Verify the medication, dose, route, time, administration record, relevant labs, and other exposures.
  3. Notify the prescriber and pharmacist; activate emergency or poison-control resources when appropriate.
  4. Carry out ordered treatment, monitoring, drug levels, ECG, laboratory testing, decontamination, or antidote.
  5. Prevent another dose by updating active orders and allergy or intolerance records through the approved workflow.
  6. Document objective findings, timing, interventions, notifications, and response in the clinical record.
  7. Complete the internal safety report according to policy and support a system-focused review.
  8. Arrange ongoing monitoring, teach-back, and follow-up before the next transition.

Do not chart blame or copy the confidential incident-report narrative into the medical record. The clinical record contains the facts and care delivered. The safety-reporting system supports learning about contributing conditions such as confusing labels, interruptions, staffing, technology, storage, handoffs, or workflow design.

External reporting and medication records

FDA MedWatch accepts reports about serious adverse events, product quality problems, therapeutic failures, and use errors involving regulated products. Follow organizational policy for who submits the report; urgent clinical care comes first. A report does not require absolute proof that the product caused the event.

Update the medication and allergy lists with precise, useful information. Do not convert nausea alone into “anaphylaxis,” and do not erase a documented severe reaction because the mechanism is uncertain. When an allergy label may be inaccurate, referral for structured evaluation can improve future options; the bedside RN does not independently challenge or remove a potentially serious allergy.

Teach-back makes the new plan usable

Ask the client or caregiver to explain the final regimen in their own words: medication and purpose, exact dose and time, what changed, what was stopped, special administration, missed-dose instructions, interactions, monitoring, refill plan, and whom to call. Separate common manageable effects from urgent warning signs. Provide an updated accessible list and encourage the client to bring it to every encounter.

Check cost, transportation, language, literacy, vision, hearing, cognition, dexterity, swallowing, storage, measuring device, and pharmacy availability. A technically correct plan that the client cannot obtain or use is not a safe transition.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Gather the complete regimen, recent changes, timing, symptoms, allergies, organ function, vital signs, labs, adherence, interacting products, and transition context.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish predictable effect, intolerance, allergy, anaphylaxis, toxicity, interaction, withdrawal, medication error, and disease progression.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise, shock, respiratory depression, severe skin or mucosal injury, dysrhythmia, bleeding, seizure, profound glucose disturbance, and acute organ failure require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Stop harmful exposure, support ABCs, obtain targeted monitoring, use protocol-directed rescue treatment, consult pharmacy and the prescriber, and resolve discrepancies.
  5. Take action: Administer emergency treatment, prevent repeat dosing, reconcile the list, document facts, communicate across settings, and report through approved systems.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, vital signs, organ function, laboratory and ECG trends, recurrence, intended therapeutic effect, list accuracy, access, and teach-back.

Clinical example

Minutes after an IV antibiotic begins, a client develops diffuse flushing, wheezing, lip swelling, vomiting, and hypotension. The RN stops the infusion, activates emergency response, supports airway and oxygenation, and gives intramuscular epinephrine under the anaphylaxis protocol rather than waiting for hives or a confirmatory test. After stabilization, the RN documents the exact drug, timing, manifestations, treatment, and outcome; updates the allergy workflow; notifies pharmacy and the prescriber; completes the safety process; and ensures the discharge plan prevents re-exposure.

Original educational synthesis. Suspected reactions, allergy documentation, medication holds, emergency treatment, antidotes, interaction management, laboratory monitoring, tapering, reconciliation responsibilities, and internal or external reporting require current drug labeling, authorized orders, pharmacist and prescriber review, facility policy, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official FDA, AHRQ, Joint Commission, or NCSBN product.
